function.name: glob_files
function.description: Recursively list workspace-relative file paths that match a glob, in sorted order. The glob is matched against each file's relative path and against its file name, using Python fnmatch rules, case-sensitive: '*' and '?' also match '/', and '[abc]' matches one listed character. It never matches file contents. Cache and VCS directories (.git, __pycache__, .pytest_cache, .mypy_cache, .ruff_cache, .tox, .venv, node_modules) are skipped.

path.description: Directory (or single file) to list under, relative to the workspace root. Default '.'.

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with 1-based line numbers. start_line and end_line are inclusive; omit start_line to begin at line 1 and end_line to read to the end. The header reports the range returned and the file's total lines. Long results are shown partially with an output id for paging.

function.name: outline
function.description: List the classes and functions of a Python file with line numbers.

function.name: search_text
function.description: Search file contents for exact text (literal characters, case-sensitive; not a regex). Returns one line per match as path:line: text, with 1-based line numbers, and states the scope searched. file_glob only selects which files are searched.

query.description: Required. The exact text to find, e.g. 'def get_real_name('.

path.description: File or directory to search, relative to the workspace root. Default '.'.

file_glob.description: Optional glob selecting files by relative path or file name (same rules as glob_files), e.g. '*.py'. It never matches file contents. Default '*'.

function.name: replace_text
function.description: Replace exact text in a file. Fails without changing the file if old_text is absent, or if it occurs more than once while replace_all is false; set replace_all to replace every occurrence. Reports how many occurrences were replaced and shows the edited lines.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Create a file, or overwrite it completely if it already exists, with the given content. Missing parent directories are created. Paths are relative to the workspace root.

function.name: run
function.description: Run one command in the workspace root without a shell: no pipes, redirection, chaining (&&, ;), cd, or variable expansion; use workspace-relative paths with forward slashes. 'python' and 'pytest' use the task's Python environment. Shows the command, status (including timeout), exit code, stdout, and stderr; long output is shown partially with an output id for paging. A successful exit does not mean the task is accepted.

function.name: read_output
function.description: Read part of an earlier tool result by its output id (for example out_12). Results that were shown partially say which id and range to request. Give start_line/end_line, or start_byte/end_byte for very long lines.

function.name: search_output
function.description: Find lines containing a literal string (plain text, not a regex) in an earlier tool result by its output id.

query.description: Required. The literal text to find.

function.name: history

function.name: glob_files
function.description: Recursively list workspace-relative file paths that match a glob, in sorted order. The glob is matched against each file's relative path and against its file name, using Python fnmatch rules, case-sensitive: '*' and '?' also match '/', and '[abc]' matches one listed character. It never matches file contents. Cache and VCS directories (.git, __pycache__, .pytest_cache, .mypy_cache, .ruff_cache, .tox, .venv, node_modules) are skipped.

path.description: Directory (or single file) to list under, relative to the workspace root. Default '.'.

The header reports the range returned and the file's total lines. Long results are shown partially with an output id for paging.

function.description: Recursively list workspace-relative file paths that match a glob, in sorted order. The glob is matched against each file's relative path and against its file name, using Python fnmatch rules, case-sensitive: '*' and '?' also match '/', and '[abc]' matches one listed character. It never matches file contents. Cache and VCS directories (.git, __pycache__, .pytest_cache, .mypy_cache, .ruff_cache, .tox, .venv, node_modules) are skipped.

message.content:
The root cause was a logic inversion bug in `sqlparse/filters/tokens.py`'s `_CaseFilter.process` (used by `KeywordCaseFilter`): it checked `if not (ttype in self.ttype)` instead of `if ttype in self.ttype`, which inverted keyword-case conversion — it changed the case of everything EXCEPT keywords, instead of changing the case of keywords. This explains all four regressions, since 'cli single file inplace', 'format: keywordcase', and 'issue469 copy as psql command' tests (and presumably a 4th related test) all exercise keyword-case formatting via the CLI or `sqlparse.format(..., keyword_case=...)`.

I fixed the condition to `if ttype in self.ttype:` so `KeywordCaseFilter` correctly converts only keyword tokens (matching the documented/expected behavior), while `IdentifierCaseFilter` is unaffected since it overrides `process` separately.

Verified manually:
- `sqlparse.format('select A, b FROM foo', keyword_case='upper')` → `'SELECT A, b FROM foo'` (keywords converted, non-keyword identifiers untouched) — correct now.
- `sqlparse.format('\\copy foo to stdout', reindent=True)` → unchanged (psql command untouched) — correct.

No other logic in the codebase referenced this inverted pattern (`not (ttype in self.ttype)` was unique to this one function), so this single fix should resolve all 4 reported regressions.

The root cause was a logic inversion bug in `sqlparse/filters/tokens.py`'s `_CaseFilter.process` (used by `KeywordCaseFilter`): it checked `if not (ttype in self.ttype)` instead of `if ttype in self.ttype`, which inverted keyword-case conversion — it changed the case of everything EXCEPT keywords, instead of changing the case of keywords. This explains all four regressions, since 'cli single file inplace', 'format: keywordcase', and 'issue469 copy as psql command' tests (and presumably a 4th related test) all exercise keyword-case formatting via the CLI or `sqlparse.format(..., keyword_case=...)`.

I fixed the condition to `if ttype in self.ttype:` so `KeywordCaseFilter` correctly converts only keyword tokens (matching the documented/expected behavior), while `IdentifierCaseFilter` is unaffected since it overrides `process` separately.

Verified manually:
- `sqlparse.format('select A, b FROM foo', keyword_case='upper')` → `'SELECT A, b FROM foo'` (keywords converted, non-keyword identifiers untouched) — correct now.
- `sqlparse.format('\\copy foo to stdout', reindent=True)` → unchanged (psql command untouched) — correct.

No other logic in the codebase referenced this inverted pattern (`not (ttype in self.ttype)` was unique to this one function), so this single fix should resolve all 4 reported regressions.

Fixed the regression: in sqlparse/filters/tokens.py, _CaseFilter.process had an inverted condition `if not (ttype in self.ttype)` that caused KeywordCaseFilter (used for the -k/--keywords CLI option and the keyword_case format option) to change the case of everything except keywords, instead of only keywords. This broke keyword-case formatting broadly, which explains the 'cli single file inplace', 'format: keywordcase', 'issue469 copy as psql command' failures (and likely a 4th keyword-case-related test), since all exercise sqlparse.format(..., keyword_case=...) or the CLI's keyword-case path.

Fix applied: changed the condition to `if ttype in self.ttype:` so KeywordCaseFilter correctly converts only Keyword tokens, leaving everything else (identifiers, psql backslash commands, etc.) untouched. IdentifierCaseFilter overrides process() separately and was unaffected.

Verified manually:
- sqlparse.format('select A, b FROM foo', keyword_case='upper') -> 'SELECT A, b FROM foo'
- sqlparse.format('select A, b FROM foo', keyword_case='lower') -> 'select A, b from foo'
- sqlparse.format('SELECT a, B from Foo', keyword_case='upper', identifier_case='upper') -> 'SELECT A, B FROM FOO'
- sqlparse.format('\\copy foo to stdout', reindent=True) -> unchanged (psql command untouched)

No other code used the inverted pattern, so this single-line fix addresses all four reported regressions without affecting other working behavior.

arguments.summary: Fixed inverted condition bug in sqlparse/filters/tokens.py's _CaseFilter.process (used by KeywordCaseFilter): changed `if not (ttype in self.ttype)` to `if ttype in self.ttype`. This was causing keyword-case conversion to apply to everything except keywords instead of only keywords, breaking CLI in-place formatting, format keyword_case option, and psql command preservation (issue469). Verified fix with manual tests for keyword_case upper/lower, combined keyword+identifier case, and psql backslash command passthrough.

message.content:
Fixed the regression: in sqlparse/filters/tokens.py, _CaseFilter.process had an inverted condition `if not (ttype in self.ttype)` that caused KeywordCaseFilter (used for the -k/--keywords CLI option and the keyword_case format option) to change the case of everything except keywords, instead of only keywords. This broke keyword-case formatting broadly, which explains the 'cli single file inplace', 'format: keywordcase', 'issue469 copy as psql command' failures (and likely a 4th keyword-case-related test), since all exercise sqlparse.format(..., keyword_case=...) or the CLI's keyword-case path.

Fix applied: changed the condition to `if ttype in self.ttype:` so KeywordCaseFilter correctly converts only Keyword tokens, leaving everything else (identifiers, psql backslash commands, etc.) untouched. IdentifierCaseFilter overrides process() separately and was unaffected.

Verified manually:
- sqlparse.format('select A, b FROM foo', keyword_case='upper') -> 'SELECT A, b FROM foo'
- sqlparse.format('select A, b FROM foo', keyword_case='lower') -> 'select A, b from foo'
- sqlparse.format('SELECT a, B from Foo', keyword_case='upper', identifier_case='upper') -> 'SELECT A, B FROM FOO'
- sqlparse.format('\\copy foo to stdout', reindent=True) -> unchanged (psql command untouched)

No other code used the inverted pattern, so this single-line fix addresses all four reported regressions without affecting other working behavior.
